row.scenario: Clone, build and load the module: the VM has its own kernel, root, Docker from boot and nested virtualisation, so nothing needs a workaround.
row.note: A hardware-virtualised Linux VM with systemd as pid 1. GPU and colocated bare metal are private enterprise offers, not public plans.

source.quote: supporting nested virtualization, FUSE, eBPF, full Linux networking and more

row.scenario: Ask for 2 vCPU / 4 GiB and get exactly that on Free; a 50 GiB disk needs Hobby, and there is no region to choose.
row.note: Any size up to the plan caps: Free 4 vCPU / 8 GiB / 32 GB, Hobby 8 / 16 / 64, Pro 32 / 64 / 256. CPU and memory resize live and only grow. No region or EU option is published.

source.quote: Every plan can create a VM at any valid size up to its CPU, memory, and disk maximums.

row.scenario: Kill the power: resume the same process tree from a paused VM, or start a fresh boot after a stop.
row.note: Pause keeps memory and processes; stop keeps the disk and drops memory; fork copies a running VM. Boot is about 65 ms, and a base snapshot starts in about a second.

source.quote: VMs provision in about 65ms from API request to ready machine.

row.scenario: Fork the running VM into three copies and try three fixes without losing the original.
row.note: Snapshots capture memory and disk, are private by default and boot in about a second. Snapshots are kept until deleted, so older ones can be chosen. No automatic backup schedule.

source.quote: Clone a running VM without pausing it — get full copies in milliseconds.

row.scenario: Write the checkpoint: up to 16 GiB per file on the VM disk, or mount an S3 bucket for shared storage; there is no separate volume.
row.note: A persistent VM keeps its disk across a stop; an ephemeral VM is deleted when it stops. Files can be read while paused. No block volume product, and no shared volume beyond an S3 bucket mounted with FUSE.

source.quote: no size limit short of 16 GiB per file

row.scenario: Leave it idle: set idleTimeoutSeconds and the VM pauses, then the next request wakes it; set −1 to keep it awake.
row.note: A paused VM resumes on the next start or on traffic that reaches it. No scheduler: cron inside the VM only runs while it runs.

source.quote: A VM paused this way resumes on its next start, or on the next traffic that reaches it.

row.scenario: Open the app: route a style.dev name to port 3000, SSH in with a scoped token, or stream a PTY to a browser you build.
row.note: Public HTTPS with managed certificates, TLS passthrough for non-HTTP, SSH through beta-ssh.freestyle.sh, and a PTY API. There is no hosted browser terminal.

source.quote: Use inbound rules to give services on your VM a public domain.

row.scenario: Serve it at your own domain: verify with a TXT record, CNAME to Freestyle, delegate the ACME challenge, and the certificate is issued.
row.note: Free style.dev subdomains need no DNS or certificate. A verified domain gets a managed certificate once _acme-challenge is delegated; single-label wildcards are supported.

source.quote: HTTPS is provisioned automatically, once _acme-challenge is delegated

row.scenario: Call the API: outbound is denied until a firewall rule allows it, and the first 50 GB (Free) or 500 GB (paid) of transfer is included.
row.note: Allowlist by domain, CIDR or identity. Default deny, so no internet until a rule allows it. Every VM shares one account-level outbound IPv4, but Freestyle does not promise it stays fixed.

source.quote: A VM gets nothing implicitly — no outbound Internet, no inbound

row.scenario: Use the key without seeing it: the edge adds the Authorization header, and the VM only holds a placeholder.
row.note: Credentials are stored encrypted at the edge and injected into outbound HTTP, Postgres or S3 requests; the VM never receives the real key. Scoped identity tokens limit an end user to named VMs and Linux users. Secrets are not exported as environment variables.

source.quote: Credential injection lets the VM authenticate without receiving the real API key or database password.

row.scenario: Drive it from your product: create a VM in the dashboard, from the CLI, or through the TypeScript SDK and REST API.
row.note: Dashboard, CLI, TypeScript SDK, OpenAPI and a PTY/file API. No MCP server. The PyPI package is the older Sandboxes SDK, not the current VM client.

source.quote: Use the freestyle CLI for interactive administration, debugging, and automation scripts.

row.scenario: Run Claude Code: it is already in the Ubuntu image, but you open the terminal and start it yourself.
row.note: Claude Code, Codex, opencode and openclaw are installed in the default Ubuntu image. No prompt API and no one-click Hermes or OpenClaw; a browser and a GNOME desktop come from guides that install them.

source.quote: claude, codex, opencode, and openclaw, also installed in the shared Node tree

row.scenario: Add a developer: create a team identity, grant one VM and one Linux user, and hand over a scoped token.
row.note: Teams, per-VM identities and tokens exist. Named roles, a dollar spend cap and usage alerts are not documented; SAML SSO, SCIM and audit logs are Enterprise-only.

source.quote: Freestyle identities let an end user or agent operate an existing VM without receiving your team API key.

row.scenario: Run 166 hours: the meter says $8.82 after allowances, but the Hobby minimum bills $50.
row.note: Per-second meter on allocated vCPU, memory and storage, with monthly allowances on every plan. No flat machine price, and no measured-CPU billing below Enterprise.

source.quote: The Hobby and Pro monthly fees are a usage credit, not a surcharge

row.scenario: Try it: the Free plan runs a light workload inside 200 vCPU-hours, 400 GiB-hours and 60,000 GiB-hours a month, with no card.
row.note: Free is a hard stop, not paid overage. The only published credit is a $5,000 deal for YC founders; there is no general signup credit.

row.scenario: Check the risk: a status page shows current state, but SOC 2, a DPA and a standard SLA are not published.
row.note: Freestyle Cloud Inc., founded in 2024, YC-backed and 5 employees per Y Combinator. A 99.99% SLA is Enterprise-only; no trust centre, SOC 2 report or DPA is published.
